questions.question: Design a chat/messaging system like WhatsApp that supports one-on-one and group messaging.
questions.title: Design a Chat/Messaging System (WhatsApp)
questions.direct_answer: Use **persistent WebSocket connections** terminated at a stateless **Connection Service** for real-time delivery, with **Kafka** as the durable message bus between services. Store messages in **Cassandra partitioned by conversation_id, clustered by message_id (time-sorted)** for ordered scans. Maintain **presence in Redis** with TTL-based heartbeats. Use **fan-out-on-write** for 1:1 and small groups, switch to **fan-out-on-read** for large broadcast channels. Server-assigned **monotonic sequence per conversation** gives ordering without distributed clocks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Real-time delivery via persistent connections, ordering and exactly-once semantics, storage partitioning, presence handling, and fan-out trade-offs at scale.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Polling HTTP for new messages, or storing messages in a relational DB partitioned by user — both collapse at WhatsApp scale.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Justify fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read by group size, explain server-assigned per-conversation sequence numbers for ordering, and acknowledge end-to-end encryption's impact on server-side features (search, abuse detection).

sections.title: Framing the Problem and What Makes This Hard
sections.content:
A chat system looks simple — "send a message, deliver it." The difficulty hides in scale and semantics:

- **Persistent connections at huge concurrency** — a billion users, ~20% online at any moment → 200M concurrent WebSocket connections. A single server holds maybe 100K, so we need ~2,000 connection servers and a way to route messages to whichever server holds the recipient.
- **Ordering is non-trivial** — "who sent first" matters, but client clocks lie. We need server-assigned sequence per conversation, not wall-clock timestamps.
- **Delivery semantics** — at-least-once is non-negotiable; messages must survive server crashes. But duplicates cause bad UX, so we also need idempotency.
- **Online/offline presence** — who's online drives UI state but updates at high frequency; can't be a hot DB row.
- **Fan-out blows up for groups** — a 1,000-member group means one send becomes 1,000 deliveries. Naive fan-out-on-write breaks at large channels.
- **End-to-end encryption** — if we do E2EE, the server can't search messages, can't run abuse detection, can't generate previews. Big product trade-off.

The core architectural decisions: **how messages flow** (push vs pull, write-fanout vs read-fanout), **how we order them** (server sequence vs vector clocks), and **how we partition storage** so a conversation's history is fast to scan.

sections.title: Clarifying Questions I'd Ask First
sections.content:
**Functional**
- One-to-one only, or also **group chats**? Max group size?
- **Media support** — images, video, file attachments? Voice/video calls in scope?
- **Read receipts** and **typing indicators** required?
- **Message search**? Across own messages or global?
- **End-to-end encryption** — in scope or server can read messages?
- **Message editing/deletion** with sync across devices?
- **Push notifications** when offline?

**Non-functional**
- **Active users and concurrency** — daily active, peak concurrent?
- **Latency budget** — sub-100 ms p99 in-region typical?
- **Multi-device** — one user, multiple sessions in sync?
- **Retention** — keep messages forever or N days? (Drives storage cost.)
- **Geographic distribution** — single region or multi-region active-active?

**Out-of-scope clarifications**
- I'd ask whether voice/video calls and stories/status are in scope, and explicitly defer them unless asked. They're separate systems.

sections.title: Assumptions I'm Locking In
sections.content:
- **1B users**, **300M DAU**, **~200M concurrent** at peak (20% of users online).
- **40B messages/day** → ~460K messages/sec average, ~1M/sec at peak.
- **Average message size**: 100 bytes (text only); media stored separately in object storage.
- **Group chat support**: up to 256 members per group (WhatsApp's limit). Broadcast channels (>1000 members) handled differently.
- **Multi-device support**: up to 4 devices per user, all kept in sync.
- **Sub-100 ms p99 in-region**, sub-500 ms cross-region.
- **Retention**: messages stored on the server until delivered to all devices; archived to cold storage after 30 days (or per user setting).
- **No E2EE in this design** — we'll discuss the trade-off but assume server-side plaintext for features like search and notifications.
- **At-least-once delivery** with **client-side dedup by message_id** — effectively exactly-once at the UI layer.

sections.title: Back-of-Envelope Capacity Estimate
sections.content:
**Throughput**

- Sends: 40B/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ **460K messages/sec average, ~1M/sec at peak**.
- Deliveries: with average group size 5 (mix of 1:1 and groups), fan-out multiplier ~3 → **~3M deliveries/sec at peak**.
- WebSocket frames: deliveries + presence + typing + receipts → **~10M frames/sec at peak**.

**Storage**

- Per message row: message_id (16) + conversation_id (16) + sender_id (8) + body (100) + timestamp (8) + flags + indexes ≈ **~250 bytes/message**.
- Daily: 40B × 250 = **10 TB/day** of message rows.
- 5-year horizon: ~18 PB. Demands a wide-column store (Cassandra/ScyllaDB/HBase) sharded across hundreds of nodes.

**Connections**

- 200M concurrent WebSockets at ~10 KB memory each (kernel + app buffers) → **~2 TB total RAM** for connection state.
- One connection server handling ~100K concurrent connections needs ~10 GB RAM → **~2,000 connection servers**.

**Bandwidth**

- Average 10M frames/sec × 200 bytes ≈ **2 GB/sec egress** — large but manageable across regions.

**Conclusion:** the bottlenecks are connection-server count and message storage I/O, not CPU. Architecture must support adding connection servers horizontally and partitioning storage by conversation.

sections.title: API Contract — WebSocket and HTTP
Data Model
sections.content:
**Cassandra** is the primary store for messages — wide rows, time-ordered scans, easy horizontal sharding.

**Messages table** (partition key = conversation_id, clustering key = message_id descending):

```cql
CREATE TABLE messages (
    conversation_id text,
    message_id      timeuuid,        -- monotonically increasing per conversation
    sender_id       text,
    body            text,
    media_ref       text,            -- S3 URL if media
    sequence        bigint,          -- server-assigned per-conversation
    sent_at         timestamp,
    PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id), message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);
```

Why this layout: scrolling history in a conversation is a single partition scan, ordered by recency. No cross-partition queries on the hot path.

**Conversations table** (partition by user_id):

```cql
CREATE TABLE user_conversations (
    user_id           text,
    last_activity_at  timestamp,
    conversation_id   text,
    last_message_id   timeuuid,
    unread_count      int,
    PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), last_activity_at, conversation_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (last_activity_at DESC);
```

Gives the inbox view (most recent conversations first) as a single partition read.

**Conversation members** (in PostgreSQL — small relational data):

| Column | Type |
|---|---|
| `conversation_id` | UUID PK |
| `user_id` | BIGINT PK |
| `role` | enum(member, admin) |
| `joined_at` | timestamp |
| `muted` | boolean |

**Presence** in Redis:

```
KEY:  presence:{user_id}
VAL:  {"status":"online","last_seen":1714000000,"connection_server":"cs-042"}
TTL:  90 seconds (refreshed by client heartbeat every 30s)
```

Relationships:

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USERS ||--o{ CONVERSATION_MEMBERS : participates
    CONVERSATIONS ||--|{ CONVERSATION_MEMBERS : has
    CONVERSATIONS ||--o{ MESSAGES : contains
    USERS {
        bigint user_id PK
        string display_name
        timestamp last_seen
    }
    CONVERSATIONS {
        uuid conversation_id PK
        enum type
        timestamp created_at
    }
    CONVERSATION_MEMBERS {
        uuid conversation_id FK
        bigint user_id FK
        enum role
        timestamp joined_at
    }
    MESSAGES {
        uuid conversation_id FK
        timeuuid message_id PK
        bigint sender_id FK
        text body
        bigint sequence
    }
```

sections.title: High-Level Architecture
sections.content:
Three logical tiers: **edge** (WebSocket termination), **services** (message processing, fan-out, presence), **storage** (Cassandra, Redis, Kafka). ```mermaid flowchart TB User1([User A]) User2([User B]) LB[Connection LB

per-shard topics}} MS[Message Service
persist + fan-out] Cassandra[(Cassandra
messages, sharded by conv_id)] Presence[(Redis
presence + sessions)] PG[(PostgreSQL
users, conv membership)] Push[Push Notification
APNS / FCM] User1 -->|WSS| LB User2 -->|WSS| LB LB --> CS1 LB --> CS2 CS1 -->|publish SEND| Kafka CS2 -->|publish SEND| Kafka Kafka --> MS MS --> Cassandra MS --> Presence MS -->|lookup conn server| Routing Routing -->|deliver| CS1 Routing -->|deliver| CS2 MS -->|offline recipient| Push CS1 -.read membership.-> PG classDef edge fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6 classDef svc fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e classDef store fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444 classDef bus fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b class CS1,CS2,LB edge class MS,Routing,Push svc class Cassandra,Presence,PG store class Kafka bus ``` **Send path:** sender's WebSocket frame → Connection Service → Kafka → Message Service → persist to Cassandra → look up recipients' connection servers in Redis → push frames out. **Why Kafka in the middle:** decouples connection servers from storage; absorbs send bursts; gives durable replay if Message Service crashes mid-fanout.

sections.title: Connection Service — The WebSocket Layer
sections.content:
Each Connection Service instance holds ~100K WebSockets and is **stateless about message content** but **stateful about connections**.

**On connect:**
- TLS handshake → authenticate via JWT → register `(user_id, device_id) → server_id` in Redis with 90s TTL
- Subscribe Kafka consumer to `deliveries.{server_id}` topic for messages routed to this server
- Start 30-second heartbeat from client to refresh Redis TTL

**On send:**
- Validate frame schema and rate-limit (50 messages/min per user)
- Publish to Kafka `messages.send.{shard}` topic, partitioned by conversation_id
- ACK back to sender with assigned sequence (returned by Message Service)

**On disconnect:**
- Remove session from Redis
- Publish presence change
- Don't lose unsent messages — sender retries on reconnect using `client_msg_id` for dedup

**Routing problem:** when User B sends to User A, how does the Message Service know which Connection Service holds User A's socket?

- Lookup `presence:{user_a}` in Redis → returns `connection_server: cs-042`
- Publish delivery frame to Kafka `deliveries.cs-042`
- cs-042 consumes and pushes through the WebSocket

**Sticky load balancing** (by user_id hash) ensures a user's reconnections land on the same server when possible — reduces churn on Redis session entries.

sections.title: Message Ordering and Delivery Guarantees
sections.content:
**Per-conversation sequence number** — server-assigned monotonic counter.

- Implemented as `INCR conv_seq:{conv_id}` in Redis (atomic) before persisting.
- Every message in a conversation has a strictly increasing `sequence`.
- Clients render messages sorted by sequence, **not by client timestamp** — timestamps are display-only.

**Why not vector clocks?** Vector clocks order events across distributed actors without a single coordinator, but they're complex, payload-heavy, and unnecessary here — we already have a coordinator (the Message Service writing per-conversation). Simpler is better.

**Why not server timestamp?** Two messages in the same millisecond on different Message Service instances would tie. Sequence is unambiguous.

**Delivery guarantees:**

- **At-least-once from server to client** — the server resends if no DELIVERED receipt arrives within 5 seconds.
- **Client dedup by `client_msg_id`** — the client tracks UUIDs it has already rendered and discards duplicates.
- **Effectively exactly-once at the UI** without distributed transactions.

**Offline handling:**

- Recipient offline → message persisted in Cassandra; not delivered now.
- Push notification fired via APNS/FCM (silent push to wake the app).
- On reconnect, client requests `GET /messages?after_seq={last_seen}` to catch up.
- Server returns all messages since the last-known sequence.

sections.title: Fan-Out — On Write vs On Read
sections.content:
Group messaging forces a choice: do you write the message into every recipient's inbox at send time, or pull on read?

| Approach | When It Wins | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Fan-out on write** | Small groups (≤ 200), 1:1 chats | Send latency includes N writes; storage cost is N× |
| **Fan-out on read** | Large channels (> 1000 members), broadcast lists | Read latency includes scanning the conversation timeline; better for write throughput |
| **Hybrid** | Production systems | Use fanout-on-write up to a threshold; switch to fanout-on-read above |

**WhatsApp/Slack reality:** they hybridize. For 1:1 and small groups, write the message into a **per-recipient inbox** (simplifies offline catchup and notification). For huge broadcast channels, store one message per channel and have clients scan the channel timeline on read.

**Our approach:** fanout-on-write for groups ≤ 256 members (matches our assumption). For broadcast channels (a separate product feature), we'd build a different read pattern.

sections.title: LLD — Class Design of the Send Pipeline
Storage Choice and Sharding
sections.content:
**Why Cassandra (or ScyllaDB) for messages**

- Single-partition reads scale linearly with cluster size; no joins needed.
- Write throughput is essentially CPU- and disk-bound, not lock-bound — perfect for our 1M writes/sec.
- Replication factor 3 with `LOCAL_QUORUM` gives us in-region durability with low latency.
- TTL columns let us automatically expire old messages without scheduled jobs.

**Sharding** — Cassandra hashes the partition key (`conversation_id`) across the ring; no manual sharding required. ~500 nodes at ~40 TB per node holds our 5-year horizon comfortably.

**Why PostgreSQL for membership**

- Conversation membership is small (<1 KB per conversation) but needs JOINs ("all conversations user X is in, with last message and unread count").
- ACID for membership operations (add user to group must be atomic).
- Throughput is small — hundreds/sec, not millions.

**Why Redis for presence**

- Read latency < 1 ms per lookup, called billions of times/day during routing.
- TTL-based expiration matches the natural "presence = recent heartbeat" model.
- Sharded Redis Cluster scales to our 200M concurrent users.

sections.title: Caching, Hot Conversations, and Read Path
sections.content:
**Recent messages cache** (Redis):

- For each active conversation, cache the last 100 messages as a Redis sorted set.
- Conversation open / scrolling within the recent window: zero Cassandra reads.
- TTL: 24 hours. Falls back to Cassandra for anything older.

**Conversation list cache** (Redis):

- For each user, cache their inbox (top 50 conversations sorted by `last_activity_at`).
- Invalidated on every new message in any of those conversations.

**Hot conversation problem** — a celebrity DM flood, or a 256-member group with constant typing:

- The `INCR conv_seq:{id}` becomes the bottleneck — single Redis key, ~50K ops/sec ceiling.
- Mitigation: pin hot conversations to a Redis server with sequence-allocation isolation, or batch sequence allocation (allocate 100 sequences at once, hand them out locally).

**Connection-side cache** — each Connection Service caches conversation membership for 60 seconds to avoid hammering PostgreSQL on every send.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Resilience
sections.content:
**Connection Service crash**

- All WebSockets on that server drop.
- Clients auto-reconnect (exponential backoff) and land on a different server via the LB.
- On reconnect, client requests `GET /messages?after_seq={last_seen}` per active conversation — catches up everything missed.
- Redis presence entry expires in 90 seconds; nothing to clean up actively.

**Message Service crash mid-fanout**

- Kafka consumer offset hasn't been committed — another instance picks up the same SendCommand and replays it.
- Cassandra write is idempotent (PRIMARY KEY = conversation_id, message_id); duplicate save is a no-op.
- Recipients may receive a duplicate frame; client dedups by `client_msg_id`.

**Cassandra node failure**

- `LOCAL_QUORUM` writes succeed as long as 2 of 3 replicas are up.
- Reads gracefully fail over to another replica.
- Replication catches up automatically when the node returns.

**Redis presence cluster failure**

- Routing falls back to **broadcast to all Connection Servers in the region**, each filtering by who they hold — inefficient (10× traffic) but functional.
- Push notifications continue working independently.

**Kafka unavailable**

- Send acknowledgement fails → client retries with same `client_msg_id`.
- Connection Service buffers a small backlog of unsent SendCommands locally.
- On Kafka recovery, backlog drains.

**Cross-region partition**

- Each region is independent for in-region traffic.
- Cross-region delivery is best-effort; messages queue and replay when partition heals.

sections.title: Observability and Security
sections.content:
**Metrics**

- `connection.count{server}` — alert if any single server > 150K (rebalance signal).
- `message.send.latency` (p50/p95/p99) — SLO < 100 ms p99.
- `message.delivery.latency` (sender-to-recipient) — the user-visible number.
- `kafka.lag{topic}` — send pipeline backpressure indicator.
- `cassandra.write.latency` and `cassandra.write.timeouts` — storage health.
- `presence.lookup.miss_rate` — catching presence inconsistencies.

**Tracing**

- Distributed trace spans the full path: Connection Service → Kafka → Message Service → Cassandra → routing → recipient Connection Service. Trace ID flows in WebSocket frame metadata.

**Security**

- **TLS 1.3** on all WebSocket connections.
- **JWT auth** on connect, refreshed by the client periodically.
- **Per-user rate limit** at Connection Service: 50 sends/min, 1000 frames/min total.
- **Input validation** — max body length, schema check, no script injection in message bodies.
- **Anti-abuse** — spam detection on send patterns; throttle suspected bots.
- **End-to-end encryption** — if E2EE is required (Signal protocol), the server sees only ciphertext. Trade-offs: no server-side search, no link previews, no abuse content scanning. WhatsApp accepts these losses; Slack and Discord don't.

sections.title: Trade-offs and What I'd Change at 10× Scale
sections.content:
**At 10× scale (10B messages/day, 2B concurrent connections):**

- **Edge-region Connection Services** — terminate WebSockets at the closest geographic point; route to the user's home region only when needed.
- **Per-region Cassandra clusters** with cross-region replication for users who roam.
- **Replace Redis presence with a gossip-based protocol** — Redis becomes a single point of contention at that scale.
- **Pull-based history fetch over QUIC/HTTP3** rather than WebSocket framing — better for large history scans.

**What I'd reconsider:**

- **Server-assigned sequence vs hybrid** — a single Redis `INCR` per conversation is fine until it isn't. Hybrid sequences (timestamp + per-conversation counter) reduce Redis pressure but complicate ordering edge cases.
- **Unified vs split storage** — separating media references from message text into different storage tiers reduces row size and Cassandra GC pressure.

**What I rejected and why:**

- **HTTP polling** — a billion users polling every 2 seconds is 500M requests/sec; impossible.
- **Long polling** — better than polling but still wastes connections compared to WebSocket.
- **Single relational DB** — ordering by partition (`conversation_id`) doesn't shard well in PostgreSQL; Cassandra was designed for this access pattern.
- **Vector clocks for ordering** — unnecessary complexity given our central per-conversation sequence allocator.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Persistent WebSockets** at stateless Connection Services with Redis-backed presence routing — the foundation of real-time delivery.
- **Kafka as the durable bus** between Connection Service and Message Service — absorbs bursts, allows replay, decouples failure domains.
- **Cassandra partitioned by conversation_id** with `message_id` clustering for time-ordered scans — native fit for the access pattern.
- **Server-assigned per-conversation sequence** for unambiguous ordering — simpler and more correct than vector clocks or client timestamps.
- **At-least-once delivery + client dedup by `client_msg_id`** — effectively exactly-once at the UI without distributed transactions.
- **Fan-out-on-write for small groups, on-read for broadcast channels** — hybrid approach matches WhatsApp/Slack production reality.
- **Push notifications via APNS/FCM** for offline recipients — the app wakes, pulls catch-up via HTTP.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Clarifying questions I'd ask first**

- One-on-one only, or also group chats — and what's the max group size?
- Media — images, video, file attachments?
- End-to-end encryption — in scope or can the server read messages?
- Read receipts and typing indicators?
- Multi-device support — one user across multiple devices in sync?
- Retention — keep messages forever or expire after N days?

**Assumptions for this design**

A billion users, 300 million daily active, around 200 million concurrent connections at peak. 40 billion messages a day, average size 100 bytes, group chats up to 256 members. Sub-100-millisecond p99 in-region. No end-to-end encryption — we'll discuss the trade-off but assume server-side plaintext.

**Quick capacity check**

- Sends: roughly 460,000 per second average, a million per second at peak
- Deliveries with average group size 5: about 3 million per second
- Storage: 10 terabytes per day of message rows — needs Cassandra or ScyllaDB sharded across hundreds of nodes
- 200 million concurrent WebSockets needs around 2,000 Connection Service instances at 100K each

**High-level shape**

- Edge layer: Connection Services terminate WebSockets, stateless about content but stateful about which user is on which server
- Bus: Kafka decouples Connection Services from the Message Service; absorbs bursts, gives durable replay
- Service layer: Message Service persists to Cassandra and orchestrates fan-out
- Storage: Cassandra for messages (partitioned by conversation_id), PostgreSQL for membership, Redis for presence

**Send path — step by step**

- Sender's WebSocket frame arrives at a Connection Service
- Connection Service publishes to Kafka, partitioned by conversation_id
- Message Service consumes, allocates a per-conversation sequence number from Redis (atomic INCR), writes to Cassandra
- ACKs sender with the assigned sequence
- Looks up each recipient's Connection Service in Redis presence; routes the delivery frame via Kafka to the right server
- Offline recipients get a push via APNS or FCM

**Ordering — server-assigned sequence per conversation**

- Every message has a strictly monotonic sequence number, allocated by Redis INCR
- Clients render by sequence, not by client timestamp — timestamps are display-only
- I rejected vector clocks because we already have a coordinator (the Message Service); they'd be unnecessary complexity
- I rejected server timestamp because two messages in the same millisecond on different instances would tie

**Delivery guarantees**

- At-least-once from server to client; the server resends if no DELIVERED receipt arrives in 5 seconds
- Client dedup by `client_msg_id` — effectively exactly-once at the UI
- Offline: message persists in Cassandra, push notification fires, client pulls catch-up on reconnect

**Data model**

- Cassandra messages table: partition key `conversation_id`, clustering key `message_id` descending — scrolling history is one partition scan
- Cassandra user_conversations table: partition by user_id, clustered by `last_activity_at` for the inbox view
- PostgreSQL conversation_members for relational membership data
- Redis `presence:{user_id}` with 90-second TTL refreshed by client heartbeat

**Fan-out — hybrid approach**

- Small groups (under 256): fan-out-on-write, message persisted into each recipient's inbox — simplifies offline catchup
- Large broadcast channels: fan-out-on-read, store one message per channel and clients scan the channel timeline
- Our design assumes ≤256 member groups, so fan-out-on-write across the board

**LLD — components in the send pipeline**

- `ConnectionHandler` — WebSocket I/O
- `MessageConsumer` — reads SendCommand from Kafka, allocates sequence, persists, fans out
- `SequenceAllocator` — wraps Redis INCR; can swap to batched allocation for hot conversations
- `MessageRepository` interface backed by Cassandra; in-memory impl for tests
- `DeliveryRouter` — per-recipient decision: online routing via Kafka, offline via push
- `PresenceService` — thin Redis wrapper

**Failure modes**

- Connection Service crash: clients reconnect, request catch-up by sequence; presence TTL cleans up stale entries
- Message Service crash mid-fanout: Kafka replay; Cassandra write is idempotent on PK; clients dedup
- Cassandra node down: LOCAL_QUORUM keeps reads and writes alive on 2 of 3 replicas
- Kafka down: small in-memory backlog at Connection Service, then 503 to client; client retries
- Redis presence cluster down: degrade to broadcast routing across all Connection Servers in the region

**Production extras**

- TLS 1.3 + JWT auth on connect, periodic token refresh
- Per-user rate limit (50 sends/minute, 1000 frames/minute)
- Distributed tracing across the full send pipeline
- E2EE if required — acknowledge that you lose server-side search, link previews, and abuse detection

**At 10× scale**

- Edge-region Connection Services for geo-proximity
- Per-region Cassandra with cross-region replication
- Gossip-based presence instead of Redis
- QUIC/HTTP3 for history pulls

**Recommendation**

**Stateless Connection Services with WebSocket termination, Kafka as the durable bus, Message Service with server-assigned per-conversation sequence numbers from Redis, Cassandra partitioned by conversation_id for messages, and APNS/FCM for offline notifications** — the same shape WhatsApp, Slack, and Discord run in production.

followup_questions: How would you implement end-to-end encryption while preserving multi-device sync — walk through the key exchange.
Walk through what happens when a user is on three devices and sends a message from their phone — how do the other two devices stay in sync?
How do typing indicators and presence updates avoid overwhelming the system if every keystroke triggered a frame?
Compare WebSocket vs gRPC streaming for the real-time channel — what would you pick and why?

Ordering is non-trivial — "who sent first" matters, but client clocks lie. We need server-assigned sequence per conversation, not wall-clock timestamps. Delivery semantics — at-least-once is non-negotiable; messages must survive server crashes. But duplicates cause bad UX, so we also need idempotency. Online/offline presence — who's online drives UI state but updates at high frequency; can't be a hot.

A single server holds maybe 100K, so we need ~2,000 connection servers and a way to route messages to whichever server holds the recipient. Delivery semantics — at-least-once is non-negotiable; messages must survive server crashes. But duplicates cause bad UX, so we also need idempotency. Online/offline presence — who's online drives UI state but updates at high frequency; can't be a hot.
Polling HTTP for new messages, or storing messages in a relational DB partitioned by user — both collapse at WhatsApp scale.

Persistent WebSockets at stateless Connection Services with Redis-backed presence routing — the foundation of real-time delivery. Kafka as the durable bus between Connection Service and Message Service — absorbs bursts, allows replay, decouples failure domains. Cassandra partitioned by conversation_id with message_id clustering for time-ordered scans — native fit for the access pattern. Server-assigned per-conversation sequence for unambiguous ordering — simpler and more correct than vector clocks or client timestamps. At-least-once delivery + client dedup by client_msg_id — effectively exactly-once at the UI without distributed transactions.
